clients.title: Connect an app
clients.intro: This vault speaks the Bitwarden protocol, so their apps work with it.
clients.setUpFirst: Set your vault up first. There is nothing for an app to sign in to yet.
clients.signInHint: On the app's sign-in screen, choose self-hosted and paste this in. Sign in with the address on your Polaris account and your master password.
clients.insecure: This address is not HTTPS. Most clients refuse to sign in over a plain connection, and they are right to - set up a certificate under Management > Domains first.
clients.extensionHint: Open it, press the settings cog on the sign-in screen, pick "Self-hosted" and paste the address into Server URL.
clients.desktopHint: Tap the region selector above the email field, choose "Self-hosted", and paste the address into Server URL.
clients.cliHint: Point the CLI at this server, then sign in as usual.
clients.letInOne: Polaris' own extension does not ask for your master password. It shows a code, you approve it here in a browser that already has this vault open, and it is handed a copy of the vault key sealed so that only it can open it.
clients.letInTwo: It opens this screen for you. Open it yourself if the extension could not, and type the code it is showing.
clients.ownOne: Built for this vault rather than adapted to it: it asks the browser for permission to talk to this address and no other, fills a login without holding any standing access to the pages you open, and locks itself again when you stop using it.
clients.ownTwo: The package for your browser is under Downloads, with the desktop app and everything else installable.
clients.signedInTitle: Apps signed in to this vault
clients.noneSignedIn: Nothing has signed in yet. An app appears here the first time it does.
clients.claimNote: The name and the kind are what each app said about itself, not something Polaris checked. If you do not recognize one, change your master password: removing a row cannot shut out something that already holds the vault key.
clients.separateTitle: If an app asks for each address separately
clients.separateHint: Some versions offer a custom environment with a field per service. These are the values.
clients.differentOne: Accounts are made in Polaris, not from a client - an app's "create account" will be refused, and your master password is separate from the one you sign in to Polaris with.
clients.differentTwo: Two-step login uses the authenticator on your Polaris account, so a code from it is what an app will ask for.
clients.differentThree: Icons for saved sites are fetched by this server rather than by Bitwarden, so the list of sites you have accounts on stays here.
clients.trademark: Bitwarden is a trademark of Bitwarden, Inc. Polaris is not affiliated with them; it implements their published client protocol.

vaults.intro: Every vault you can open, each with its own key. Yours is the first.
vaults.empty: Nothing here yet. Set up your own vault from the Vault app first; then you can make another to keep something apart, or to share it with somebody.
vaults.newIntro: Its key is made in this browser and wrapped to you. The name is the one thing about it the server can read.
vaults.ownBody: Everything you save lands here unless you put it somewhere else. It is yours alone: nobody can be let in, because the key is wrapped under your master password and nothing on the server can derive it.
vaults.ownShare: To let somebody at one of these items, make a vault below and move the item into it from the item itself. Moving re-encrypts it under that vault's key, which is what sharing actually is here.
vaults.orgNoVault: {name} has no vault yet, and setting one up is not something your role there can do.
vaults.setUpIntro: The keys are made in this browser. You will hold it first, and anybody else who should read it has to be let in by somebody who already can.
vaults.removeBody: They keep whatever they already synced - a key cannot be un-given - but they stop receiving anything new. Change what they knew if that matters.
vaults.deleteCollectionBody: What is in it is not deleted. It stops being shared through this collection, which may leave it reachable only by an administrator.
vaults.leaveBody: It stops syncing to you and you lose what is in it. Whatever you already synced stays on the devices that have it.
vaults.deleteVaultBody: Everything in it goes with it, and its key goes too. Anybody you let in keeps what they already synced. This cannot be undone.
vaults.waiting: You are on this vault's list but nobody has let you in yet. Until somebody who holds its key vouches for you, there is nothing here to read - which is what makes it worth being in.
vaults.collectionsIntro: Where an item in this vault lives. Moving something into one is done from the item itself.
vaults.membersIntro: Adding somebody puts them on the list. Letting them in hands over the key, and only somebody who already holds it can do that.
vaults.noVaultYet: {name} - no vault of their own yet
vaults.scopeIntro: They are handed this vault's key either way. What you choose here is what they are shown and allowed to change.

vaults.deleteHint: Deleting it takes everything in it, and its key.

settings.argon2: Argon2id - harder to attack, slower to unlock
settings.samePassword: That is your Polaris password. If they are the same, whoever learns one has the vault as well.
settings.deleteBody: Every item in it goes with it, and nobody - not an administrator - can bring it back. Export first if you want to keep anything.
settings.iconsBody: Items can show the icon of the website they belong to. Off by default, because it is not only a preference: the icon is fetched from that website, by this browser, so a site that receives the request learns somebody with a Polaris vault has an account there. It never goes through Polaris and never through an icon service - either of those would hand over every domain in a vault nobody is supposed to be able to read.
settings.appsBody: End every app's session without changing your password. They will each ask for it again.
settings.timeoutBody: Your key is held by this browser, never by the server. This is how long it may keep it while you are not using the vault.
settings.timeoutNote: Anything but the first choice keeps the key in this tab's own storage, which is cleared when the tab closes. It is never written to disk and never sent anywhere.
settings.wrongCurrent: That is not your current master password.
settings.changed: Your master password has changed. Every app will ask for it again.
settings.title: Vault settings
settings.intro: Everything here needs your master password, and does its work in this browser.
settings.polarisPasswordHint: Checked so the two passwords cannot end up being the same one.
settings.kdfHint: Changing this re-derives your key, so it happens with the password.
settings.iconsSwitch: Fetch website icons in this browser
settings.appsSignedOut: Every app has been signed out.
settings.timeoutSaved: Saved. Your vault was locked so the new setting applies.
settings.timeoutLabel: How long the vault stays open
settings.deleteHint: Everything in it goes. Your Polaris account stays as it is.

setup.polarisPasswordHint: So Polaris knows it is you, and so it can check the two passwords are not the same one.
setup.samePassword: That is your Polaris password. If they are the same, whoever learns one has the vault as well - which is the one thing the vault is for.
setup.understand: I understand that forgetting this password means losing everything in the vault.
setup.understandNote: Not even an administrator can reset it. That is what makes it worth using.
setup.noCrypto: Your browser could not create the keys. It needs a secure connection.
setup.title: Set up your vault
setup.intro: Your master password unlocks everything in it, and it never leaves this browser.
setup.hintNote: Shown to anybody who asks for it at sign-in, so keep it oblique.
setup.hintLeaks: That hint contains the password itself.

port.skipped: {count, plural, one {# shared item was left out: you do not hold the key for it yet.} other {# shared items were left out: you do not hold the key for them yet.}}
port.exportIntro: Every item, in the clear. That is what makes it portable, and what makes it worth deleting once whatever you are moving to has read it.

formats.json: Bitwarden JSON - everything, and what its clients read

formats.keepass: KeePass XML - for KeePass and KeePassXC

port.importIntro: A Bitwarden JSON export, a KeePass XML export, or the CSV most managers and browsers write. The file is read here and every item is encrypted before it is sent.
port.kdbxNote: A KeePass .kdbx is the database itself rather than an export. In KeePass, use File > Export and pick KeePass XML.

refusals.noColumns: That file has no username, password or notes column.
refusals.encrypted: That export is encrypted. Export it again unencrypted.
refusals.protected: That export still has its passwords protected. In KeePass, export again with protection off.
refusals.badXml: That file is not readable XML.
refusals.notKeePass: That XML is not a KeePass export.
refusals.kdbx: A .kdbx is a KeePass database, not an export. In KeePass, use File > Export and pick KeePass XML or CSV.

port.emptyFile: There was nothing in that file.

folders.intro: Yours alone. The names are encrypted with everything else, so nobody else can read them.
folders.deleteBody: What is in it stays in your vault; it just stops being filed here.

move.title: Move "{name}"
move.intro: It is re-encrypted here under the key of wherever it goes. Everybody in that vault will be able to read it, and anybody who already synced it keeps the copy they have.
move.nowhere: There is nowhere to move it. Make another vault, or ask somebody to let you into theirs.
move.noKey: You do not hold the key for that vault.

qr.noCamera: The camera is not available here. Browsers only allow it over a secure (https) address - upload a screenshot of the code instead.
qr.notFound: No code was found in that picture. A tighter crop usually does it.
qr.notPicture: That file could not be read as a picture.
